title: Learning Transferable Graph Structures via Geometric Alignment
one_liner: A graph model learns to align local coordinate frames across different graphs so that the same substructures work everywhere.
lead: Foundation models (pre-trained models adapted to new tasks) have succeeded in text and images, but graphs present a puzzle: the same substructures (triangles, star patterns) appear in many graphs, yet we do not know if they are truly learnable in a way that transfers to new tasks. This paper asks: when you learn a substructure from one graph, will it help you understand a different graph? The authors answer by learning not just the substructure itself, but how to rotate and scale the numerical coordinate systems at each node so the same substructure takes on the same numerical form everywhere.

problem.h2: Why common graph patterns do not travel between graphs
paras: A network is a graph: nodes are things, edges are connections. In a social network, a triangle is three friends who all know each other. In a protein graph, a triangle is three molecules linked together. But if you teach a model what a triangle looks like when represented as numbers in a social graph, and then show it a protein graph, the model does not recognize the same triangle pattern. The reason: the same three-node connection is represented by very different sets of numbers in the two graphs.

A naive first attempt: train a model on one graph by learning weights (numbers that control how the model responds). Then apply those same weights to a new graph. This fails because the input numbers in graph A represent nodes in completely different ways than the input numbers in graph B. The weights are tuned to recognize patterns in graph A's specific numbers. On graph B's different numbers, the same weights produce nonsense.

callout.b: The core problem in one sentence.
callout.html: The same three-node connection has totally different numbers in social networks versus protein networks, so weights trained on one cannot recognize it in the other.

paras: Standard graph models train the weights for node features directly. This paper instead learns how to rotate and scale the local coordinate frames at each node so that the same geometric patterns appear in the same form across different graphs. The object is the local coordinate transformation (not the weights themselves, but the geometric alignment).

hidden.h2: How aligned the local number systems are
hidden.name: Local frame alignment score
paras: The paper introduces a hidden quantity: how much the numbers at one node are related to the numbers at neighboring nodes in a consistent, predictable way. Imagine each node has a rotation (a twist) applied to its numbers. If all neighboring nodes twist in a compatible way, the numbers flow smoothly across the graph and the same pattern appears in the same numerical form everywhere. If the twists contradict each other, numbers jump around randomly and patterns will look different in different places.

The paper measures this using a penalty called the Dirichlet loss, which penalizes contradictory rotations between neighbors. High penalty means neighboring nodes' twists disagree; low penalty means they agree. The model learns to reduce this penalty by making all nodes' number twists globally compatible, so that any learned pattern (such as detecting three-node connections) works everywhere because the numerical representation of that pattern is now the same everywhere.

heat.caption: Darker means more aligned with neighbors. Highlighted nodes have compatible local number twists.

reads.html: Alignment is whether neighboring nodes' number systems rotate and scale together consistently. If they do, a learned pattern detector works everywhere because the pattern is always in the same numerical form.

The model learns a local rotation at each node (called a bundle of directions, a mathematical structure capturing how each point relates to its neighbors). The Dirichlet loss penalizes neighboring nodes whose rotations disagree, ensuring that all rotations form one globally compatible system.

mechanism.h2: Why learning aligned coordinates enables transfer
paras: Here is the causal chain: A substructure is a relationship between three nodes. In a social graph, three friends might be numbered [1, 2], [3, 1], [2, 3]. In a protein graph, the same three-molecule connection might be numbered [100, 200], [300, 100], [200, 300]. The three-node pattern is identical, but the numbers are completely different. A naive model trained to recognize the social numbers will fail on the protein numbers.

The paper's key insight: instead of learning fixed weights for a fixed set of numbers, learn a rotation (a mathematical transformation that twists the coordinate axes) at each node. Each node applies a rotation to its numbers so they align with its neighbors' rotated numbers. When all nodes in a graph apply compatible rotations, the substructures are now always represented in the same canonical numerical form. Training a pattern detector on this canonical form means the detector works in any other graph as long as you apply the same rotations. The Dirichlet loss keeps the rotations consistent across the entire graph; low loss means the rotations are globally compatible, guaranteeing transferability.

stages.s: Graph with node features in different numerical scales
Define a rotation at each node that aligns its numbers with neighbors
Minimize Dirichlet loss to make all rotations globally compatible
Train pattern detector on the rotated canonical coordinates
Pattern detector that works across graphs with no retraining

math.words: Total cost equals the substructure learning cost plus a penalty for each edge where the neighboring nodes' rotations do not match.

how strongly to penalize misaligned rotations; higher lambda forces stricter alignment
how much the two nodes' rotations differ (measured as an angle)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Graph has 4 nodes forming a chain A-B-C-D (3 edges). Each edge has a rotation difference.
Edge A to B: rotations differ by 0.3 radians. Penalty: 0.3 times 0.3 = 0.09
Edge B to C: rotations differ by 0.8 radians. Penalty: 0.8 times 0.8 = 0.64
Edge C to D: rotations differ by 0.2 radians. Penalty: 0.2 times 0.2 = 0.04
If lambda is set to 2.0, the alignment cost contributes 2.0 times 0.77 equals 1.54 to total loss.
During training, the model adjusts rotations to shrink this. Large misalignments are expensive, so the model makes all rotations compatible.

math.note: This formula makes the model strongly prefer globally compatible rotations across the entire graph, enabling transfer.

bars.h2: How transfer works compared to naive training

charts.title: Naive: train on one graph, test on another
charts.note: Weights learned on the first graph do not recognize the same structures in new graphs with different coordinates.

charts.title: This paper: aligned geometry transfer
charts.note: By aligning the geometric frames, the learned substructure detectors recognize the same patterns in new graphs immediately.

items.html: If the training and test graphs have fundamentally different types of connections (e.g. a social network has sparse local neighborhoods; a protein network has dense cliques), alignment cannot fix the mismatch. The geometric mismatch is too large.

If the lambda tuning knob is too low, the model learns frames that locally align but globally contradict. A triangle points north on one side of the graph and south on the other. Substructure detectors trained on one side fail on the other.

items.b: Rare substructures drown out the signal.
items.html: If the new graph has only a few examples of the substructure to transfer, the model cannot validate whether its learned pattern truly works. Noise can look like signal.
When the graph types are related and lambda is tuned so that frame alignment is smooth and global, the learned substructure detectors generalize without retraining.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build two small graphs with the same local substructure repeated in different geometric forms. Example: create a social network with 50 nodes where every triangle has coordinates in range [0, 10], and a second network with 50 nodes where the same triangle patterns appear in range [100, 200]. Train the model to find triangles in the first graph using coordinate alignment. Then test on the second graph without retraining. The demo should show that the model still finds the triangles accurately because the learned geometric alignment generalizes.
demo.metric_eq: Transfer accuracy = (triangles found in new graph) / (triangles actually present in new graph)
demo.closing: The demo must show that the learned rotations (not random weight guessing) enable transfer, because the rotations make the numerical representation of triangles identical in both graphs. Show before-and-after: naive weights fail on the new graph's different numbers, but the learned rotations transform both graphs' numbers so triangles look identical, so the pattern detector works immediately.
